variants.note: Ridge runs the long dimension; the defining_characteristics record this outright.
The integral or added lean-to (catslide) is 'the normal growth move after about 1660' per massing_affinities -- a later state of the same house, not a different roof design.
A Dutch and Hudson Valley device, not part of the English-derived First Period repertoire.
A classical-tradition roof form; absent from the medieval-derived frame vocabulary this style draws on.
A Second Empire form, over a century after this style's floruit.
Incompatible with a steep structural roof and the exposed frame it carries.

roof_form.rule: Side-gable, ridge running the long dimension of the frame bay; the saltbox/catslide profile is the same house after its rear lean-to addition, not a separate design.

roof_pitch.rule: Rise:run between 10:12 and 14:12 (40-50 degrees, own constraint c02): steep enough that the roof itself is doing structural work, but resolved narrower here than the family's generic 45-degree-and-up floor because 40-45 degrees is also attested and the 50-55 degree band the family's medieval-british ancestor allows for a thatch or stone-slate roof does not apply -- this style's covering is split shingle.
roof_pitch.note: Specified rather than extends: medieval-british's inherited 45-degree floor and this node's own hard constraint (c02, 40-50 degrees / 10:12-14:12) disagree at the low end, and the family rule's own reasoning is keyed to a heavy thatch or stone-slate roof this style never actually built in. Restating avoids a resolved kit that quietly carries a wrong lower bound.

variants.note: Split (riven) shingle -- the actual covering.
The steep pitch preserves the proportion the thatched English original needed, but the style's own description is explicit that thatch itself 'was never actually used here.'
No documented use; the covering is split shingle.
No documented use; the covering is split shingle.
No local slate industry serving this floruit; reserved for later, grander work.
Anachronistic to the family's floruit.
A 17th-century rafter foot lands on the plate rather than past it; there is no applied cornice to speak of.

The boxed cornice arrives in the 18th century as applied joinery, not as part of the frame, and its appearance is one of the better date markers available on a First Period house (per this style's own proportion-pack rationale).

eave_condition.rule: Window heads within a few inches of the eave, with no frieze band; the eave is flush with the frame until the boxed, returned cornice of applied 18th-century joinery starts to appear.

variants.note: Its appearance on an otherwise First Period massing is one of the clearer single dating tells the type offers.
The framed overhang (jetty) with carved drop pendants at the gable, as at the Parson Capen House -- an urban and higher-style pre-1700 device, not universal.
No classical order before c. 1710 (defining_characteristics).
A masonry-envelope device; this style's gable is a clapboarded frame end.
The English parent shows its frame; New England covers it entirely in clapboard because exposed infill does not survive the freeze-thaw climate (distinguished_from: english-medieval-timber-frame).

chimney.rule_append: Exactly one stack, positioned within the plan rather than at a gable end -- own hard constraint c01 -- with a base not less than 7 ft square and typically 8-12 ft, occupying roughly a third of the plan depth; the front door opens directly against this mass rather than into a passage.
chimney.note: Extends the family's inherited 'oversized and prominent' rule (from british-vernacular) with the actual count, position and size this style fixes and the family does not: the British ancestor explicitly leaves count and position to the style level because its two members disagree, and this is that resolution.

variants.note: Oak post-and-beam with summer beam, gunstock posts and mortise-and-tenon joinery, entirely clad in clapboard; the family's default framing method here, not merely one option among several.
This branch of the family builds in frame; masonry is confined to the chimney mass, never the envelope.

Riven or sawn, 4-5 in exposure on the weather elevation.
5-6 in exposure on the coast (own constraint c05).
The frame is covered entirely, never exposed (distinguished_from: english-medieval-timber-frame).
'No masonry veneer' (defining_characteristics).
'No masonry veneer' (defining_characteristics).

Not part of this style's envelope vocabulary; the wall is clapboard or shingle over frame.

primary_cladding.rule: Riven or sawn clapboard at 4-5 in exposure on the weather elevation (up to 6 in elsewhere), or shingle at 5-6 in on the coast; no masonry veneer anywhere.

material_change_rule.rule: One cladding material covers the whole envelope from sill to eave on every elevation; the only masonry on the building is the chimney mass, which is never veneered onto the frame and never treated as a decorative material change at grade or at a storey line.
material_change_rule.note: Editorial synthesis of 'no masonry veneer' (defining_characteristics) with the absence of any documented storey-line material break in the sources given; not a separately sourced rule.

belt_course.rule: No belt or string course. 'There is no moulding anywhere except a chamfer and its stop' (style description); a belt course is a classical device this style's own ancestor (medieval-british) already forbids at the apparatus level, and nothing in the envelope group revives it.

corner_quoin.rule: No quoin. Frame construction gives the corner nothing to quoin, and the classical vocabulary quoins belong to is absent before c. 1710.

variants.note: Consistent with the style's near-total absence of applied trim before 1700.

corner_board.note: Editorial inference from the style's stated absence of moulding before 1700, not a directly quoted corner-board source.

frieze.rule: No frieze band of any width. Own hard constraint c03: a frieze over 4 in converts the elevation to Georgian, and the diagnostic reading for this style is precisely that the window head sits close under the plate with nothing between them.

parapet.rule: No parapet on a steep gabled roof carried on a visible eave.

variants.note: Diamond-quarry leaded lights; glass imported and taxed, so openings stay small.
Counterweighted sash arrives about 1700.

height_to_width.note: Own proportional_system: opening 2'6"-3'4" wide by 4'0"-5'6" high. Set by the casement and frame bay, not a treatise ratio -- narrower than the family's own bound sash-light pack's 1.85-2.6 measured band.

window_proportion.rule: Openings run close to 1:1.7 (height:width), set by the casement and the frame bay rather than by any pattern-book proportion.

variants.note: Own constraint c04: six-over-six on a First Period massing is an anachronism of at least fifty years.
The casement sits flush under the plate with nothing over it.
No classical order before c. 1710.
No classical order before c. 1710 (defining_characteristics).
Colonial Revival tell.
Wide trim with a backband is the Colonial Revival tell (distinguished_from: colonial-revival), not the original.
A fully classical assembly, absent before c. 1710.
A fully classical assembly, absent before c. 1710.

special_window.rule: No palladian, lunette, oculus, or diocletian window. These are Georgian- and revival-era markers that postdate this style's own floruit and are among the clearest tells that a Georgian door or window has been added to a First Period house (distinguished_from: georgian-colonial-american).

variants.note: Own defining_characteristics: 'after 1700 a modest entry frame,' the one ornamental exception the style allows.

transom_sidelight.rule: No transom or sidelight. These belong to the classical frontispiece Georgian influence introduces after about 1720 (distinguished_from: georgian-colonial-american) and have no place on an unadorned First Period door.

variants.note: Matches the style's own additive, accretive growth logic (wing_strategy): a later structure added at a distance, the way a lean-to or outshot was added, rather than composed into the front.
A garage door on the entrance elevation contradicts the near-symmetrical, chimney-centred front this style's own composition_parti depends on.
A 19th-century device, centuries after this style's floruit.

garage_strategy.note: No historical precedent exists for any traditional style (docs/inheritance.md); this is authored to be consistent with the style's own additive massing logic, not retrieved.

entry_sequence.rule: One threshold: the exterior door opens directly into a lobby barely large enough to close the door behind you, hard against the chimney base, with no intervening hall -- from the lobby the visitor turns immediately left or right into a heated room. 'The entry is not a hall but a porch' (style description).

under_summer_beam.note: 6 ft 8 in - 7 ft 6 in; own proportional_system figure.

ceiling_height_rule.rule: Ceiling height is measured to the underside of the exposed summer beam, not to the joists: 6 ft 8 in to 7 ft 6 in under the beam, 7 ft 0 in to 8 ft 0 in between beams. A modern adult reads the room with the beam at eye level.

profile_family.value: exposed frame with a chamfered arris and a carved chamfer stop; no applied moulding profile family

trim_family.rule: There is no moulding anywhere except the chamfer and its stop -- lamb's-tongue, ogee, or taper -- which is the one decorative decision the carpenter made and, per the style's own description, the one he made carefully.

crown.rule: No interior crown or cornice moulding; the ceiling is either the exposed joists or a plain plastered surface meeting the summer beam directly.

chair_rail.rule: No chair rail. The style's applied interior trim is confined to the chamfer stop; a chair rail is a later classical convention.

variants.note: 'A cramped winder squeezed between the stack and the front door' (style description).

stair_type.rule: A tight, boxed winder stair occupying the lobby beside the chimney mass, not a straight run with landings.

variants.note: Southern colonial or post-1740 Georgian (own diagnostic_tells).
Contradicts own hard constraint c01: exactly one chimney, positioned within the plan, not at a gable end.
Dutch and French colonial.
Contradicts own hard constraint c01: a single central stack, not distributed hearths.

hearth_position.rule: Exactly one hearth mass, central in the plan, serving fireplaces back-to-back in the rooms that flank it -- own hard constraint c01.

stair_position.rule: In the lobby entry, immediately beside the chimney mass and against the front door -- the same cramped space the plan's only threshold occupies.

variants.note: The rear lean-to (saltbox) addition, common after about 1660.
Requires the paired-interior-chimney plan Georgian influence brings; incoherent with a single central stack.

daylight_strategy.rule: Light comes in small hard patches from windows set high and tight under the plate; the fire end of the room is bright and warm and the far corner is cold and dark. Glass is a luxury import and the strategy is conservation, not composition.

street_relationship.rule: The house sits in a clearing, not on a street, and has no urban face: it is symmetrical only by accident of the chimney's centrality, the front carries the five-bay composition and the rear and gable ends may carry little or nothing. Settlement was against a scarce, cleared lot, not a platted frontage.
